title: Haemorrhagic shock - response to resuscitation

related.why: trauma secondary survey (different phase of trauma care)

brief.scenario: You are the core surgical trainee attending the major trauma bay. A 29-year-old motorcyclist was struck by a car 35 minutes ago. His pulse is 132/min, BP 102/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, capillary refill 5 seconds; he is cold and confused.
brief.task: The examiner will supply changes in observations and point-of-care findings. Explain your immediate priorities, response to resuscitation and destination for definitive haemorrhage control.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Haemorrhagic shock is a physiological process, not a number or an ATLS class alone.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Giving repeated large crystalloid boluses and scanning a deteriorating non-responder instead of controlling bleeding.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Activate trauma and major haemorrhage response; treat external bleeding and perform cABCDE.

flow: Control accessible bleeding and assess for internal bleeding.
Establish access, activate blood products and administer time-appropriate TXA.
Classify response and choose definitive haemorrhage-control pathway.

grid.label: Recognition of shock
grid.fail: Reassures because one BP is nearly normal.
grid.borderline: Notes tachycardia but misses mental-state and perfusion abnormalities.
grid.pass: Recognises haemorrhagic shock from mechanism, perfusion, pulse, BP and mental status.
grid.high: Emphasises occult shock and trend-based physiology rather than rigid shock-class labels.

grid.label: Primary survey
grid.fail: Starts detailed secondary survey before addressing ABC threats.
grid.borderline: Calls help but does not prioritise airway, chest and circulation.
grid.pass: Runs cABCDE with airway protection, breathing assessment and bleeding control.
grid.high: Coordinates team and ensures repeated assessment during intervention.

grid.label: Haemorrhage control
grid.fail: Attempts to normalise BP with repeated large crystalloid boluses.
grid.borderline: Applies pressure but overlooks suspected pelvic bleeding.
grid.pass: Applies direct pressure and indicated pelvic binder, urgent definitive haemorrhage control.
grid.high: Explicitly prioritises early interventional radiology/surgery based on bleeding site and physiology.

grid.label: Access and sampling
grid.borderline: Places one line without activating major haemorrhage pathway.
grid.pass: Obtains two large-bore IV/IO access, blood sampling/crossmatch and activates major haemorrhage protocol.
grid.high: Coordinates balanced component therapy, warming and rapid lab reassessment.

grid.label: Resuscitation approach
grid.fail: Delays blood while pouring in crystalloid.
grid.borderline: Requests blood but cannot interpret ongoing response.
grid.pass: Restricts crystalloid, prioritises blood products and assesses response and ongoing bleeding.
grid.high: Explains transient versus non-response and avoids permissive hypotension with significant TBI.

grid.label: TXA and coagulopathy
grid.fail: Misses time-sensitive TXA or prescribes it beyond the limit indiscriminately.
grid.borderline: Knows TXA may help but not the injury-time qualification.
grid.pass: Gives TXA 1 g IV over 10 min as soon as possible (within 3 h of injury), then 1 g over 8 h per protocol; addresses temperature, calcium, coagulation.
grid.high: Tracks time from injury, supports lab/viscoelastic-guided haemostasis when available.

grid.label: Decision to investigate
grid.fail: Sends persistent non-responder to CT before haemorrhage control.
grid.pass: Uses eFAST/bedside assessment as appropriate; arranges urgent haemorrhage control rather than delayed CT in non-responder.
grid.high: Explains when CT is appropriate for a responding/stable patient and re-evaluates frequently.

grid.label: Communication and command
grid.fail: Does not summon trauma team or share situation.
grid.borderline: Calls registrar but omits physiological risk or plan.
grid.pass: Calls trauma/anaesthetic/surgical teams; gives focused structured handover.
grid.high: Names intervention owner, blood bank liaison and clear contingency if collapse continues.

grid.label: Reassessment and transfer
grid.fail: Stops monitoring after initial BP improvement.
grid.borderline: Rechecks BP alone and misses ongoing perfusion concern.
grid.pass: Reassesses physiology, bleed control, response to products and transfer to definitive care.
grid.high: Anticipates temperature, coagulopathy and rapid return to theatre/IR if rebleeding.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: A 29-year-old motorcyclist was hit by a car 35 minutes ago. Pulse 132, RR 28, capillary refill 5 seconds, cool skin, confused, BP 102/66.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The pressure is 102/66, so this looks stable enough for a CT first.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will do a detailed secondary survey and then reassess.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: There is heavy bleeding from a thigh wound and pelvic pain.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Leave the leg bleeding until the scan identifies everything.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Blood pressure falls to 78/42. eFAST is negative; pelvis is tender.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Give two litres of crystalloid first. There is no need to call the blood bank yet.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: After the crystalloid his BP briefly rises to 94/58, but his pulse climbs to 148 and he becomes drowsy.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The blood pressure came up after the fluid, so he is responding and the haemorrhage is controlled.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Do you have a haemorrhage-control plan?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: We can discuss TXA after investigations.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I have not called the major trauma team because the mechanism is common.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will move on before repeating observations.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This patient has haemorrhagic shock despite an initially measurable blood pressure: tachycardia, poor perfusion, confusion and high-energy injury. I will activate the major trauma and major haemorrhage pathways.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: There is severe bleeding from the thigh and suspected pelvic injury. What is your first sequence?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: cABCDE, maintain cervical spine precautions, assess airway and breathing, give oxygen if indicated, and control life-threatening bleeding immediately.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Apply firm direct pressure to the thigh; if uncontrolled life-threatening limb bleeding persists, use a tourniquet. Use a pelvic binder correctly positioned over the greater trochanters if active pelvic bleeding is suspected.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: BP is now 78/42 and his pulse 148. There is no clear external improvement.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Two large-bore IVs or IO access, samples including FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, blood gas and group/crossmatch; activate and liaise with blood bank for the major haemorrhage protocol.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Prioritise blood products and restrict large-volume crystalloid. I will track mentation, pulse, BP, perfusion and response continuously. A transient improvement is not haemorrhage control.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Injury was 35 minutes ago. Can you use tranexamic acid?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes. With active or suspected major traumatic bleeding at 35 minutes, give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes now, then 1 g IV infused over 8 hours, per the local major haemorrhage protocol; it must start within three hours of injury. Prevent hypothermia and monitor coagulation.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: eFAST is negative. Should the patient proceed to CT?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not while a persistent non-responder. A negative eFAST does not exclude pelvic or retroperitoneal bleeding. I will coordinate urgent definitive haemorrhage control with trauma surgery and interventional radiology.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will give a structured handover: injury and timing, haemodynamic trend, interventions, transfusion, suspected source and immediate destination.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: A colleague asks whether to accept a low blood pressure if the patient also has severe brain injury.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It depends on which injury dominates. NICE NG39 (2016): in combined haemorrhagic shock and traumatic brain injury, use restrictive volume resuscitation if haemorrhage dominates, and less restrictive resuscitation to maintain cerebral perfusion if brain injury dominates, with senior-directed targets.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Recheck temperature, ionised calcium, clotting, bleeding and response during transfer and keep the trauma leader updated.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: We have a suspected uncontrolled haemorrhage. Shock is evident from tachycardia, delayed refill and altered consciousness even before pressure crashes. Activate trauma call and major haemorrhage now.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: A motorcyclist arrived 35 minutes after a collision. BP 102/66, HR 132, RR 28, capillary refill 5 seconds, cool and confused.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will allocate airway and breathing assessment to colleagues while I lead catastrophic-bleeding control and circulation. Repeat cABCDE after every change.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: There is brisk thigh bleeding and an unstable-looking pelvis.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Apply pressure immediately; use a tourniquet if a life-threatening limb bleed is not controlled. A correctly sited pelvic binder is appropriate for suspected pelvic haemorrhage. We must avoid repeated provocative pelvic examination.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Please place large-bore vascular access or IO if delayed, take crossmatch and coagulation samples, request blood products and liaise directly with the transfusion lab. Warm the patient and blood.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: After transient improvement with initial resuscitation he deteriorates to 78/42, HR 148. eFAST is negative.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He is a transient responder progressing towards non-response. I will not chase a normal blood pressure with litres of saline. Continue haemostatic resuscitation with blood components according to the major-haemorrhage protocol, reassess bleeding source and arrange definitive control.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What if he also has a severe traumatic brain injury?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: We would not tolerate the same restricted-pressure target. Severe TBI requires maintenance of cerebral perfusion, with anaesthetic and trauma leadership setting appropriate goals.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: His injury was 35 minutes ago: give TXA now for suspected active major bleeding, ensure warming, and monitor coagulation, fibrinogen, calcium and blood gas. We must not postpone definitive haemorrhage control for a perfect panel.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Negative eFAST is not reassurance about pelvic or retroperitoneal sources. A non-responder needs urgent theatre or haemorrhage-control pathway; CT is for patients with sufficient physiological stability and appropriate transfer support.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: My handover to the trauma consultant and anaesthetist is: high-energy collision, progressive shock, thigh and suspected pelvic bleeding, interventions and blood products underway, transient response, request immediate definitive haemorrhage control.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will reassess after every unit and intervention, watch for hypothermia and coagulopathy, document the trend and confirm the receiving team and destination.

failures.move: Missing clinical shock because initial systolic BP is above 90
Leaving uncontrolled life-threatening external bleeding without pressure or appropriate tourniquet
Substituting repeated large crystalloid boluses for early blood products
Sending a persistent non-responder to CT instead of pursuing urgent haemorrhage control
Applying permissive hypotension indiscriminately to severe TBI

recovery.when: If his pressure seemed to rule out shock
recovery.line: His pressure does not rule out shock; I am escalating now and will reassess perfusion while we control bleeding.

recovery.when: If you mistook a transient response for stabilisation
recovery.line: This is a transient response, not definitive stabilisation; I need major haemorrhage resuscitation and immediate senior-led source control.

knowledge.fact: Major trauma bleeding requires direct pressure and selected use of tourniquets or pelvic binders.

Give IV tranexamic acid as soon as possible for active or suspected major traumatic bleeding: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g infused over 8 hours, per the local major haemorrhage protocol; not after three hours unless hyperfibrinolysis is present.
Major traumatic bleeding requires protocols for blood products and rapid reversal of relevant anticoagulants.
Restricted fluid strategy applies only in selected trauma patients without severe brain injury; adequate cerebral perfusion is important with severe TBI.
Pelvic stabilisation and urgent haemorrhage-control interventions are central for ongoing pelvic bleeding.
The initial approach should prioritise haemorrhage source control with repeated physiological reassessment.

recall.think: Shock can be present before profound hypotension.
recall.say: “Activate major trauma and the major haemorrhage protocol; bleeding control is urgent.”
do: cABCDE, compression/binder when indicated, vascular access, blood products, TXA.

numbers.meaning: restricted SBP 80–90 mmHg is a conditional European trauma target without brain injury, not a universal target.

recall.trap: Transient BP improvement does not mean bleeding stopped; do not indiscriminately use permissive hypotension with TBI.
recall.finish: Confirm response category, destination for bleeding control and structured handover.

partner.opening: This is the major trauma bay. He is cold, confused and tachycardic.

reveals.finding: Time since injury 35 minutes. External thigh wound actively bleeding; suspected pelvic injury. No medication history initially known.

reveals.trigger: Cue 1: After initial interventions (this is not revealed at the start)
reveals.finding: BP falls to 78/42 and HR 148; eFAST negative.

push.question: Examiner asks about severe concomitant TBI and permissive hypotension only after candidate has discussed transfusion.
Why not take him straight to CT? The eFAST is negative.
push.expect: Do not suggest CT for persistent haemodynamic non-response; definitive pathway is senior-led.
